fields.definition: The stronger, sharper onset transient of a note played with a dynamic accent, in which the attack portion is emphasized so the note's leading edge is louder and more pronounced than the surrounding unaccented notes.
fields.plain_english: An accent attack is the extra-strong start of a note that a player hits harder on purpose. It makes the beginning of that note pop out louder than the notes around it.
fields.purpose_function: It marks which notes carry rhythmic or musical emphasis, shaping groove and phrasing. Recognizing it helps a technician keep that emphasis instead of flattening it during dynamics processing.
fields.practical_application: When mixing, a technician uses gentle or slow-attack compression and careful transient shaping so accented hits keep their punch and still stand out from the rest of a part.
common_mistakes: Using a fast compressor attack that clamps the accented transient and erases the emphasis.
Confusing an accent attack (a dynamic emphasis on the note's start) with a brighter tone or added EQ.
Over-limiting a part until accented and unaccented notes all sound the same.
scenario_contexts: Keeping accented snare hits punchy while compressing a drum bus.
Preserving accented notes in a bass or piano line during mastering.
Editing a MIDI performance so accented beats keep higher velocity and a stronger attack.

sources: Samuel Adler, The Study of Orchestration (articulation and accents)
David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (attack transients and dynamics)
Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook (transients and dynamics)

fields.definition: Unwanted mechanical noise produced by an instrument's action, the moving mechanism that transfers a player's touch to the sound-producing element, such as key, hammer, damper, or pallet movement in pianos, keyboards, and organs; it is captured as clicks, thumps, or clatter alongside the intended tone.
fields.plain_english: Action noise is the clicky, mechanical sound an instrument's moving parts make, like piano keys and hammers working. A microphone can pick it up along with the music, even though it is not the note itself.
fields.purpose_function: Naming it lets a technician separate the wanted musical sound from mechanical racket. It exists as a recording and maintenance concern because too much action noise distracts from the performance.
fields.practical_application: When recording piano or organ, a technician chooses mic placement and distance to reduce action noise, and flags a worn or poorly regulated action that needs servicing.
common_mistakes: Blaming the microphone for action noise when the real cause is a worn or poorly regulated instrument action.
Placing a mic right over the keys or hammers, which captures the most action noise.
Trying to EQ out action noise after the fact instead of fixing placement or the instrument first.
scenario_contexts: Close-miking a grand piano and hearing hammer and key noise in quiet passages.
Recording a pipe or electronic organ where key and pallet action is audible.
A pianist's pedal and damper mechanism adding thumps to a solo take.

sources: Kawai Musical Instruments - technical support documentation (keyboard and piano action noise)
David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (piano recording and mic placement)
Glen Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (acoustic instruments and mechanical noise)

fields.definition: A brief, sudden blast of moving air reaching a microphone that produces a transient thump or overload, such as a vocal plosive, a breath or wind gust, or the puff of air at the onset of a wind-instrument note.
fields.plain_english: An air burst is a quick puff or blast of air that hits the mic and makes a sudden thump. It happens with hard 'p' and 'b' sounds, a gust of wind, or a sharp breath.
fields.purpose_function: Identifying it helps a technician stop air blasts from thumping or overloading a channel. It matters because a strong air burst can distort the signal or ruin an otherwise good take.
fields.practical_application: A technician fits a pop filter or foam windscreen, adjusts mic angle, and may add a high-pass filter to tame air bursts on vocals and on outdoor or wind sources.
common_mistakes: Singing or speaking straight into the mic with no pop filter, so plosive air bursts thump the diaphragm.
Confusing an air burst (a physical puff of air on the capsule) with electronic clipping.
Removing air bursts only with EQ instead of preventing them with a screen and better mic angle.
scenario_contexts: A vocalist's hard 'P' plosive thumping a large-diaphragm condenser.
Wind gusts hitting a mic during an outdoor live event.
The breath burst at the start of a flute or reed note.

sources: Yamaha Sound Reinforcement Handbook (microphones, windscreens, and plosives)
David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (pop filters and plosives)
DPA Microphones - technical application notes (wind and pop protection)

fields.definition: Broadband rushing or hissing noise caused by moving air reaching a microphone, coming from wind, ventilation and HVAC airflow, fans, or a performer's breath, and heard as an unwanted low-level rush behind the intended sound.
fields.plain_english: Air noise is the soft rushing or hissing sound made by moving air, like wind, a fan, or an air vent. A mic can pick it up as an unwanted background rush under the real sound.
fields.purpose_function: Naming it helps a technician track down and reduce noise caused by airflow rather than by electronics. It matters because air noise raises the background level and hurts clarity.
fields.practical_application: On the job a technician uses windscreens outdoors, turns off or baffles HVAC and fans, and positions mics away from air currents to keep air noise out of a recording.
common_mistakes: Leaving HVAC or a computer fan running near the mic and blaming the hiss on the preamp.
Confusing air noise (from moving air) with electronic hiss (from gear and gain).
Using no windscreen outdoors, then trying to fix heavy air noise in the mix.
scenario_contexts: An air-conditioning vent adding a steady rush to a quiet studio take.
Wind across a boom mic on an outdoor shoot.
A close vocal mic catching breath rush between phrases.

sources: Yamaha Sound Reinforcement Handbook (wind noise and windscreens)
Glen Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (microphone environment and noise)
Shure - technical support and application notes (wind and handling noise)

fields.definition: A harmonic on a string instrument produced by stopping the string firmly with one finger while another finger lightly touches a nodal point above it, most commonly a perfect fourth higher to sound a flute-like tone two octaves above the stopped note; unlike a natural harmonic, it can be produced on a stopped (fingered) string at any pitch.
fields.plain_english: An artificial harmonic is a high, bell-like note on a string. The player holds one finger down and lightly touches the string with another. Both fingers move as a pair, so the player can sound these pure tones at almost any pitch.
fields.purpose_function: It lets players reach very high, pure, bell-like pitches beyond normal fingering and adds a special glassy color. It exists to extend the range and timbre of violins, guitars, and related strings.
fields.practical_application: A technician recognizes the soft, high, pure tone of an artificial harmonic when miking or mixing strings, and takes care to capture its quiet level and delicate attack cleanly.
common_mistakes: Confusing an artificial harmonic (touching a node on a stopped string) with a natural harmonic (touching an open string).
Expecting a loud sound; artificial harmonics are quiet and need careful gain and placement to record well.
Reading the touched note as the pitch you hear, when the sounding harmonic is much higher.
scenario_contexts: A violinist playing high artificial harmonics in an orchestral passage.
A classical guitarist using artificial harmonics for a bell-like melody.
Miking a string quartet where soft harmonics must stay audible in the mix.

sources: Samuel Adler, The Study of Orchestration (string harmonics)
Walter Piston, Orchestration (harmonics on strings)
The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (harmonics)

fields.definition: A subjective timbre descriptor for a harsh, aggressive, honking quality in the lower midrange, typically a forceful, cutting attack from brass, reeds, saxophone, or an overdriven source, in which the sound seems to "bark" out with a hard, nasal edge.
fields.plain_english: "Bark" describes a harsh, honking, aggressive sound, like a sax or trumpet blasting out with a hard edge. It is the sound seeming to snap or shout at you.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a technician a quick word for an aggressive, honking midrange they may want to boost for attitude or tame for smoothness. It helps aim EQ at the right midrange.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may add bark to a horn or guitar with an upper-mid EQ boost for aggression, or cut around 400 Hz to 1 kHz to reduce an unwanted honk.
common_mistakes: Confusing timbral 'bark' (an aggressive honk) with the Bark scale, a separate psychoacoustic frequency scale.
Adding so much upper-mid bark that a horn or guitar becomes harsh and fatiguing.
Blaming the source for bark when a resonant room or mic peak is causing the honk.
scenario_contexts: Describing a punchy, aggressive baritone sax as having bark.
Dialing bark into a rock guitar so it cuts through a dense mix.
Cutting a honky midrange peak so brass stops barking.

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook (glossary of descriptive terms)
Glen Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (timbre and midrange character)
ProSoundWeb - Glossary of Commonly Used Sound/Audio Terms

fields.definition: Mechanical noise, ranging from low-frequency rumble to a high-pitched whine or grinding, produced by worn, dry, or damaged bearings in rotating equipment such as tape-machine motors and capstans, turntable platters, cooling fans, and hard drives; it can radiate into a room or couple into the signal path.
fields.plain_english: Bearing noise is the rumble, whine, or grinding made by worn-out bearings in spinning parts, like motors, fans, or a turntable. As a bearing wears, the smooth spin turns rough and noisy.
fields.purpose_function: Identifying bearing noise points a technician to a specific worn part that needs cleaning, lubrication, or replacement. It matters for quiet operation and for preventing equipment failure.
fields.practical_application: A technician traces a rumble or whine to a motor, capstan, or fan bearing, then services or replaces it to restore quiet, smooth operation and keep the noise out of recordings.
common_mistakes: Ignoring early bearing whine until the bearing seizes and damages the motor or shaft.
Confusing mechanical bearing noise with electrical hum or hiss in the signal path.
Over-oiling a sealed or self-lubricating bearing instead of replacing a worn one.
scenario_contexts: A tape machine's capstan bearing adding rumble to playback.
A turntable platter bearing producing low-frequency rumble picked up by the cartridge.
A noisy cooling fan bearing whining inside an amplifier or console.

sources: Glen Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (mechanical noise and motors)
David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (rumble and mechanical noise)
Studer/Revox tape machine service manual documentation (capstan and motor bearing service)

fields.definition: The sharp, high-frequency click at the very start of a bass-drum (kick) note, produced when the beater strikes the batter head, especially with a hard felt, plastic, or wood beater; it forms the attack transient that gives the kick definition and helps it cut through a mix.
fields.plain_english: Beater click is the sharp little "click" you hear at the start of a kick-drum hit, made by the pedal beater striking the head. A hard beater gives more click, which helps the kick punch through a loud mix.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the attack and articulation that let a kick drum be heard clearly, especially on small speakers and in busy arrangements. Engineers manage it to balance punch against boom.
fields.practical_application: An engineer adds or emphasizes beater click with a boundary or beater-side mic, a hard beater, or an EQ boost around 2 to 5 kHz so the kick stays audible in the mix.
common_mistakes: Boosting beater click so hard the kick sounds clicky and thin instead of full and punchy.
Confusing beater click (the attack transient) with the low-end thump or boom of the drum.
Removing all click with EQ, leaving a kick that disappears on small speakers.
scenario_contexts: Adding beater click to a metal kick so it cuts through distorted guitars.
Swapping to a hard plastic beater for more click in a live show.
EQ-boosting the click region so a dance kick reads on phone speakers.

sources: David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (drum recording and kick attack)
Sound on Sound - kick drum recording and mixing technique
Bobby Owsinski, The Recording Engineer's Handbook (drum miking)

fields.definition: The percussive slapping or smacking transient heard when a bass-drum beater strikes and momentarily rests against the batter head, giving a harder, broader attack than a fine click; it is most prominent with hard beaters and a buried-beater pedal technique.
fields.plain_english: Beater slap is the hard smack sound of the kick pedal's beater hitting the drumhead. It is a bigger, broader attack than the thin click, more like a slap than a tick.
fields.purpose_function: It supplies an aggressive, punchy attack that helps a kick feel powerful and tight, especially in rock and metal. Engineers use it to add impact and articulation to the drum's front edge.
fields.practical_application: An engineer captures beater slap with a hard beater and close mic placement, or shapes it with transient tools, to give the kick a strong slapping attack without losing low-end weight.
common_mistakes: Pushing beater slap so hard the kick sounds slappy and loses its low-end body.
Confusing beater slap (a broad attack smack) with a thin high-frequency beater click.
Relying on slap alone for punch while ignoring the drum's tuning and low-end tone.
scenario_contexts: Getting an aggressive slapping kick attack for a metal track.
Using a buried-beater technique for a tighter, slappier kick.
Balancing beater slap against sub-low weight on a rock drum bus.

sources: David Miles Huber & Robert Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (bass drum miking and beater)
Sound on Sound - kick drum sound and beater choice
Bobby Owsinski, The Recording Engineer's Handbook (drum miking and attack)
